title: Westsource Group Holdings (Mar 2018 FCA) SR&ED Ruling
subject: Federal Court of Appeal review of a Tax Court decision denying SR&ED credits for industrial product development.
summary: Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2018 FCA 57, confirms that Canadian corporations claiming SR&ED deductions and investment tax credits under the Income Tax Act must complete every technical narrative field on their own Form T661 within 12 months of the filing-due date; blank fields are fatal, even if the Minister already holds the information.
metaDescription: Read the March 2018 Federal Court of Appeal decision for Westsource Group Holdings regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit appeals.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2018 FCA 57, affirming the judgment of the Tax Court of Canada in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 9, stands as a foundational precedent in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) jurisprudence. While the majority of SR&ED litigation in Canada centres on substantive scientific eligibility—evaluating whether claimed activities satisfy the statutory definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act")—Westsource addresses the critical intersection between substantive technical disclosures and mandatory procedural compliance. Specifically, the ruling establishes that the technical project narratives requested on Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and its accompanying Schedule 60 (T2SCH60) constitute statutorily mandated "prescribed information" under subsections 37(11) and 37(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Act. A taxpayer's failure to populate those technical narrative fields on the prescribed form prior to the expiry of the statutory 12-month reporting deadline is fatal to the claim, even where the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") already possesses the exact technical information through a related corporation's accepted SR&ED filing or prior-year returns.
Factual Matrix and Procedural History

The appellant, Westsource Group Holdings Inc. ("Westsource"), was a privately held corporation based in Saskatchewan whose primary business activity consisted of providing management services to its operating subsidiary and affiliated companies, including a related corporation, WestSource Solutions Inc. When Westsource originally filed its T2 corporate income tax return for the 2011 taxation year, it did not include any claim or information regarding SR&ED activities. The Minister initially assessed Westsource's 2011 taxation year by notice dated July 11, 2012.

Subsequently, prior to the expiry of the 12-month SR&ED reporting deadline following its corporate filing-due date for the 2011 taxation year, Westsource submitted an amended tax filing containing Form T661 and Schedule 60 to claim refundable investment tax credits (RITCs) in respect of two SR&ED projects: Project 1, for which Westsource claimed an RITC of $29,504, and Project 2, for which Westsource claimed an RITC of $26,894. On Schedule 60 of Form T661 (corresponding to Part 2, Section B – Project Descriptions of Form T661), Westsource properly completed all required fields for Project 2, providing the requisite technical descriptions in Boxes 240, 242, and 244. However, for Project 1, Westsource left Boxes 240, 242, and 244 entirely blank.

On the version of Form T661 applicable to the 2011 taxation year, these three boxes requested the core technical narrative required to evaluate whether a project satisfied the statutory definition of SR&ED. Box 240 required a description of the scientific or technological advancement sought by the project. Box 242 required a description of the scientific or technological obstacles or uncertainties that had to be overcome to achieve that advancement. Box 244 required a description of the work performed—specifically, the systematic investigation or search carried out in the taxation year by means of experiment or analysis—to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainties described in Box 242. In subsequent administrative revisions to Form T661 by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the former Box 240 was restructured so that on modern versions of Form T661, the three mandatory technical narrative questions are situated at Line 242 (scientific or technological uncertainties), Line 244 (work performed in the tax year to overcome those uncertainties), and Line 246 (scientific or technological advancements achieved or attempted).

Westsource's position regarding the blank Boxes 240, 242, and 244 for Project 1 was that the missing information was not important to its particular claim because the Minister was already in possession of the relevant information: a corporation related to Westsource, WestSource Solutions Inc., had participated in the same project, and Westsource's own form stated that the project was a continuation from a prior year. WestSource Solutions Inc. had filed its own Form T661 in respect of the same project—which Westsource argued contained the information missing from its own form—and the Minister had accepted WestSource Solutions Inc.'s claims for that project.

Upon reviewing Westsource's 2011 SR&ED claim, the Minister allowed the $26,894 RITC for Project 2 in full. However, the Minister disallowed Project 1 and denied the corresponding $29,504 RITC without conducting a substantive technical review of Project 1, on the sole ground that Westsource failed to file a prescribed form containing the "prescribed information" within 12 months of its filing-due date as mandated by subsections 37(11) and 37(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Act. Westsource did not submit the missing narrative information for Boxes 240, 242, and 244 prior to the expiry of the 12-month statutory filing period.

Westsource appealed the assessment to the Tax Court of Canada under the General Procedure. On January 24, 2017, Justice Valerie A. Miller dismissed the appeal (2017 TCC 9), holding that every piece of information requested on Form T661 is "prescribed information" authorized by statute, and that the technical descriptions in Boxes 240, 242, and 244 are essential to determining whether an activity qualifies as SR&ED. Westsource subsequently appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal.
Governing Statutory Framework

The legal dispute in Westsource is governed by an interlocking series of provisions within the Income Tax Act (Canada) that regulate both the substantive definition of SR&ED and the procedural conditions precedent to claiming SR&ED expenditure deductions and investment tax credits. Subsection 248(1) of the Act defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement, as well as specified support work (such as engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research) where the work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core research. In Canadian tax jurisprudence—anchored by the seminal decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) and reaffirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2022)—substantive eligibility under subsection 248(1) is evaluated through five cumulative questions: whether there was a scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be removed by standard practice or routine engineering; whether the claimant formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; whether the overall approach adopted was consistent with the scientific method, including systematic testing and modification of hypotheses; whether the process was undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement; and whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.

To translate eligible research into tax relief, subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to deduct, in computing income from the business for a taxation year, an amount not exceeding the taxpayer's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures of a current nature incurred in Canada. However, access to subsection 37(1) is strictly conditioned upon compliance with subsection 37(11), which stipulates that, subject to subsection 37(12), a taxpayer must file with the Minister a prescribed form (designated by the Minister as Form T661) on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. Under paragraph 37(11)(a), this prescribed form must contain "prescribed information in respect of the expenditure", and following legislative amendments enacted in 2013, paragraph 37(11)(b) additionally requires "claim preparer information" as defined in subsection 162(5.3). Because the definition of "filing-due date" in subsection 248(1), read with paragraph 150(1)(a) of the Act, sets a corporation's filing-due date at six months after the end of its taxation year, subsection 37(11) establishes an absolute 18-month statutory window from the end of a corporation's fiscal year to file a complete Form T661.

The statutory consequences of failing to satisfy subsection 37(11) are draconian. Subsection 37(11.1) provides that, subject to subsection 37(12), if the prescribed information in respect of an expenditure referred to in paragraph 37(11)(a) is not contained in the prescribed form filed within the subsection 37(11) deadline, no amount in respect of the expenditure may be deducted under subsection 37(1). Crucially, subsection 37(12) enacts a comprehensive deeming rule whereby any expenditure in respect of which the taxpayer fails to comply with subsection 37(11) is deemed, for the purposes of the entire Income Tax Act, not to be an expenditure on or in respect of scientific research and experimental development.

A parallel statutory bar governs Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under section 127, which are claimed by corporations on Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) and may be refundable as RITCs under section 127.1 for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations. First, because subsection 37(12) deems a non-compliant expenditure not to be an SR&ED expenditure for all purposes of the Act, the expenditure automatically ceases to qualify as a "qualified expenditure" for ITC purposes. Second, paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) independently reinforces this preclusion, stipulating that no amount shall be included in computing a taxpayer's ITC in respect of an expenditure unless the taxpayer files with the Minister a prescribed form containing prescribed information in respect of the amount on or before the day that is one year (12 months) after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year.
Final Holding of the Federal Court of Appeal

On March 21, 2018, a unanimous three-judge panel of the Federal Court of Appeal (comprising Justices Rennie, Woods, and Laskin), with Justice Judith Woods delivering Reasons for Judgment from the Bench at Toronto, Ontario, dismissed Westsource's appeal with costs. Recognizing that whether Westsource complied with statutory filing requirements despite leaving three boxes blank raised a question of law, the Court applied the appellate standard of correctness. The Federal Court of Appeal held that the language of the Income Tax Act is clear and unambiguous, and that "prescribed information" unequivocally encompasses the technical project descriptions requested in Boxes 240, 242, and 244 of Form T661 and Schedule 60, as this information is necessary to determine whether the claimed activity qualifies as SR&ED. Furthermore, the Court held that the statutory scheme strictly requires the claiming taxpayer itself to provide that information directly on the prescribed form within the statutory deadline, regardless of whether the Minister already possessed the relevant technical details from a collaborating related corporation's tax return or prior-year filings, and confirmed that the Courts possess no jurisdiction to grant relief from statutory filing conditions on the basis of fairness alone.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of Westsource's SR&ED claim for Project 1 resulted from a convergence of four distinct legal, procedural, and structural deficiencies. A granular examination of these failures illustrates how procedural omissions on Form T661 legally extinguish substantive R&D tax credit rights in Canada.
Omission of Substantive Eligibility Narratives on the Face of the Prescribed Form

The primary evidentiary and procedural failure in Westsource was the complete omission of technical narratives in Boxes 240, 242, and 244 of Schedule 60 (Form T661, Part 2, Section B) for Project 1. In Canadian SR&ED administration, Form T661 is not a mere financial summary schedule; rather, it is a bifurcated legal instrument comprising both financial expenditure schedules (Parts 3, 4, 5, and 6) and a mandatory technical pleading (Part 2, Sections A, B, and C). As counsel for the Crown emphasized and both the Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal accepted, the information requested in Boxes 240, 242, and 244 "goes to the heart of whether the claim made is SR&ED".

Each of these three boxes directly maps onto the statutory elements of subsection 248(1) and the Northwest Hydraulic legal test. Box 240 (now Line 246 – Scientific or Technological Advancement) establishes the purposive threshold of subsection 248(1), demonstrating that the work was undertaken to generate new scientific knowledge or a technological advancement that advances the taxpayer's underlying technological knowledge base beyond standard industry practice. Box 242 (now Line 242 – Scientific or Technological Uncertainty) establishes the existence of a system-level or component-level technological uncertainty or obstacle that could not be resolved through publicly available scientific knowledge, standard engineering routines, or off-the-shelf methodologies. Box 244 (now Line 244 – Work Performed in the Taxation Year) establishes the execution of a "systematic investigation or search" by means of experiment or analysis during the specific fiscal period, detailing the formulation of hypotheses, experimental testing protocols, data analysis, and logical conclusions reached in the taxation year.

By leaving Boxes 240, 242, and 244 blank on Schedule 60 for Project 1 while populating only the project title, continuation indicator, and financial expenditure lines, Westsource severed the financial claim from its statutory technical predicate. The instructions on Form T661 explicitly state that "[t]he information requested in this form and documents supporting your expenditures are prescribed information". Under Justice Miller's analysis in 2017 TCC 9, affirmed by Justice Woods in 2018 FCA 57, when Parliament requires a taxpayer to file a "prescribed form containing prescribed information" under subsection 37(11), every field on the form authorized by the Minister that is required to evaluate the claim constitutes "prescribed information". Without text in Boxes 240, 242, and 244, the Minister could not perform an initial screening review to determine with reasonable confidence whether Project 1 met the definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1).
The Fallacy of "Constructive Possession" in Intra-Group Collaborative R&D

The second critical failure in Westsource arose from a fundamental misunderstanding of corporate personality and intra-group SR&ED documentation under the Income Tax Act. Westsource contended that its omission of Boxes 240, 242, and 244 was immaterial because the Minister was already in actual possession of all relevant technical information regarding Project 1. Specifically, Westsource relied on two contextual facts: first, that its related corporation, WestSource Solutions Inc., had participated in Project 1, had filed its own Form T661 for that project, and had its claims for that project accepted by the Minister; and second, that Westsource's own Schedule 60 indicated that Project 1 was a continuation of a project claimed in a prior taxation year.

The Federal Court of Appeal summarily rejected this "constructive possession" doctrine. Under the Income Tax Act, each corporation—regardless of whether it is a parent holding company, a management corporation, or a wholly owned operating subsidiary within a related or associated corporate group—is a separate and distinct taxpayer obliged to file its own return of income under paragraph 150(1)(a) and its own Form T661 under subsection 37(11). This legal separation carries profound technical and evidentiary consequences in collaborative R&D arrangements. Even when two related corporations collaborate on a single overarching engineering or R&D initiative, the specific activities, personnel, and expenditures incurred by the management holding company differ from the activities and expenditures incurred by the operating subsidiary. Box 244 (now Line 244) specifically requires the claimant to describe the work performed in the taxation year by that claimant (or on its behalf) to overcome the technological uncertainties. A related company's Form T661 narrative describes the related company's work, not necessarily the specific systematic investigation or directly attributable support work performed by the management holding company.

Similarly, checking a box on Form T661 indicating that a project is a continuation from a prior taxation year cannot substitute for completing Boxes 240, 242, and 244. Under subsection 37(1) and section 127, SR&ED eligibility is determined on an annual, taxation-year-by-taxation-year basis. While the overarching technological advancement sought (Box 240 / Line 246) may span multiple fiscal years, the specific technological obstacles encountered and hypotheses formulated during the current fiscal year (Box 242 / Line 242) and the specific experimental work performed during the current 12-month taxation year (Box 244 / Line 244) must be freshly articulated for each taxation year claimed. Justice Woods held at paragraph 11 of 2018 FCA 57 that "[t]he problem with this submission is that the legislative scheme is clear. The information must be provided by the taxpayer on the prescribed form". The Minister is under no legal obligation to cross-reference the tax returns of affiliated corporations, search historical audit files from prior taxation years, or piece together an incomplete claim from external sources held within the CRA's databases.
Misplaced Reliance on Extrinsic Budgetary Materials Over Unambiguous Statutory Text

In attempting to salvage its claim before the Federal Court of Appeal, Westsource mounted a purposive statutory interpretation argument rooted in extrinsic legislative history. Westsource argued that what is encompassed by "prescribed information" in subsection 37(11) was ambiguous in both the legislation and administrative policy statements, and should therefore be interpreted flexibly to support R&D activity. In support of this contention, Westsource cited budgetary material from which, it submitted, the purpose of the filing requirement could be gleaned: simply to deny retroactive claims for these tax incentives. On that basis, Westsource submitted that the Minister's restrictive approach to interpreting prescribed information was not appropriate, given that the purpose of the SR&ED legislation is to encourage research and development activity.

The Federal Court of Appeal dismantled both prongs of this argument, reinforcing strict principles of Canadian tax statutory interpretation. While Justice Woods acknowledged that encouraging R&D is one legislative objective of the SR&ED regime, the Court emphasized that another key legislative objective enacted by Parliament in subsections 37(11) and 37(12) is to facilitate efficient tax administration by strictly denying tax incentives if filing requirements are not satisfied. In Canadian tax law, incentive provisions do not override clear statutory conditions precedent. Applying textual, contextual, and purposive analysis, the Federal Court of Appeal concluded that the legislation is not ambiguous and that its interpretation of prescribed information is consistent with the administrative policy statements to which the Court was referred. As Justice Woods wrote at paragraph 9, "[a] general statement of legislative intent in budget material cannot take precedence over clear language in the legislation. In this case, the legislation is not ambiguous – the information that was missing from the form was required to be included". Consequently, tax practitioners cannot rely on Department of Finance explanatory notes or budget speeches to narrow the scope of mandatory fields on CRA prescribed forms.
Incurable Expiry of the 18-Month Statutory Bar and the Absence of Equitable Relief

The fourth failure—and the procedural trap that made Westsource's omission permanently fatal—was the interaction between Westsource's late-stage filing workflow and the absolute deeming mechanism of subsections 37(11.1), 37(12), and paragraph 127(9)(m). Westsource initially filed its 2011 T2 return without an SR&ED claim, and only submitted its Form T661 by way of amendment later in the 12-month reporting period following its filing-due date. By the time the CRA processed the amended filing and disallowed Project 1 due to the blank Boxes 240, 242, and 244, the 12-month deadline under subsection 37(11) had expired.

In Canadian SR&ED law, the 12-month post-filing-due-date deadline (18 months after fiscal year-end for corporations) operates as an absolute statutory bar. Unlike ordinary business expense deductions under section 9 or 18 of the Act—which can be substantiated with additional documentation during a CRA audit, at the Notice of Objection stage before the CRA Appeals Division, or at trial before the Tax Court of Canada—an SR&ED expenditure under subsection 37(11) cannot even enter the substantive eligibility inquiry unless the prescribed form containing all prescribed information was filed before the statutory deadline expired. Once that deadline passes without Boxes 240, 242, and 244 (now Lines 242, 244, and 246) being populated, subsection 37(12) conclusively deems the expenditures not to be SR&ED expenditures for all purposes of the Act. Neither the Minister nor the Tax Court of Canada possesses discretionary authority to extend the subsection 37(11) deadline, and as the Federal Court of Appeal reiterated at paragraph 11, even where the result seems harsh in a taxpayer's particular circumstances, "relief cannot be provided on the basis of fairness alone".

A structural comparison within section 37 and section 162 of the Act further underscores Parliament's deliberate severity regarding Part 2 technical narratives. When Parliament amended subsection 37(11) in 2013 to add paragraph 37(11)(b)—requiring "claim preparer information" in Part 9 of Form T661—Parliament specifically drafted subsection 37(11.1) so that the disallowance of the SR&ED deduction applies only if the prescribed information referred to in paragraph 37(11)(a) ("prescribed information in respect of the expenditure", which includes Part 2 project descriptions) is missing. Omissions in Part 9 regarding claim preparer billing arrangements do not invalidate the SR&ED claim; instead, they trigger a $1,000 administrative penalty under subsection 162(5.1), for which the claimant and claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable (subject to a due diligence defence for the preparer under subsection 162(5.2)). This statutory bifurcation proves that Parliament intentionally reserved total forfeiture of SR&ED deductions and ITCs for omissions of paragraph 37(11)(a) prescribed project and expenditure information.

Furthermore, Westsource exposes a severe latent risk in the CRA's administrative "Top 20 Projects" filing policy. Under Section 4.1 of the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, claimants with more than 20 SR&ED projects in a taxation year are administratively permitted to transmit Part 2 project descriptions for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value when filing Form T661, provided they report the project costs for all claimed projects in Part 6 and complete and maintain at their place of business a completed Part 2 of Form T661 for every single project claimed, ready to be submitted upon CRA request. In light of Westsource, if a multi-project claimant submits only 20 Part 2 narratives and fails to have complete Part 2 forms prepared for the remaining projects upon request—or if an administrative error omits the Part 2 text for any project—the CRA has binding appellate authority under 2018 FCA 57 to automatically disallow the expenditures for any project lacking a completed Part 2 narrative.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and administrative legal requirement examined in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen (2018 FCA 57) and Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 9) against the taxpayer's specific compliance failure and the governing judicial standard of proof established by the Courts.

headers: Governing Judicial Standard & Burden of Proof (2017 TCC 9 / 2018 FCA 57)

cells: ITA Subsections 37(11), 37(11.1) & 37(12): Mandatory filing of a prescribed form (Form T661) containing "prescribed information in respect of the expenditure" within 12 months after the taxpayer's paragraph 150(1)(a) filing-due date.

Westsource filed an amended 2011 return with Form T661 and Schedule 60 within the 12-month window, but left Boxes 240, 242, and 244 on Schedule 60 completely blank for Project 1 ($29,504 RITC), while completing them only for Project 2 ($26,894 RITC).

Strict Statutory Condition Precedent (Correctness Standard): All information requested on Form T661 that is necessary to determine whether an activity qualifies as SR&ED is statutorily "prescribed information". Failure to populate Boxes 240, 242, and 244 by the 12-month deadline triggers the absolute deeming bar in subsection 37(12), deeming the costs not to be SR&ED expenditures.

ITA Subsection 127(9), Definition of "Investment Tax Credit", Paragraph (m): Precludes inclusion of any qualified expenditure in ITC calculations unless the prescribed form containing prescribed information is filed within one year (12 months) after the filing-due date.

Westsource claimed a $29,504 RITC on Schedule 31 in respect of Project 1 expenditures without providing the corresponding prescribed project descriptions on Schedule 60 of Form T661 within the one-year post-filing-due-date window.

Absolute Bar to ITC Entitlement: Compliance with both subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) is mandatory to generate a valid ITC or RITC. Absent timely filing of the technical narrative on Form T661, the Minister is legally required to deny the ITC without conducting a substantive technical audit of the project.
Form T661, Part 2, Section B – Box 240 (Now Line 246) & ITA Subsection 248(1): Mandatory disclosure of the scientific or technological advancement sought or achieved by the project.
Left Box 240 entirely blank for Project 1; failed to articulate on Form T661 how Westsource's management or engineering activities sought to advance the underlying technological knowledge base.

Prima Facie Disclosure on the Prescribed Form: The claimant must explicitly articulate the technological advancement sought (within the 350-word limit on modern Line 246) directly on its own Form T661 so the CRA can assess eligibility under subsection 248(1).
Form T661, Part 2, Section B – Box 242 (Now Line 242) & ITA Subsection 248(1): Mandatory disclosure of the scientific or technological obstacles or uncertainties faced.
Left Box 242 entirely blank for Project 1; provided no narrative identifying system-level or component-level technological uncertainties that could not be resolved by standard practice.

Heart of the SR&ED Inquiry: Identifying technological uncertainty (within the 350-word limit on modern Line 242) goes to the core of whether SR&ED exists under Northwest Hydraulic. Blank fields fail to establish any threshold uncertainty on the prescribed form.
Form T661, Part 2, Section B – Box 244 (Now Line 244) & ITA Subsection 248(1): Mandatory disclosure of the systematic investigation or search (experiment or analysis) performed in the taxation year.

Left Box 244 entirely blank for Project 1; failed to describe the specific hypotheses tested, experiments conducted, or directly attributable support work performed by Westsource during the 2011 taxation year.

Taxation-Year and Taxpayer-Specific Narrative: The claimant must detail on Form T661 (within the 700-word limit on modern Line 244) the systematic investigation performed in that specific taxation year by that specific taxpayer.

Corporate Entity Separation in Collaborative R&D & Multi-Year Projects (ITA Subsections 2(1), 37(11), 150(1)(a)): Each corporation must file its own complete Form T661 substantiating its own claimed expenditures for the year.

Relied on the fact that related collaborator WestSource Solutions Inc. had already filed a complete, accepted Form T661 for Project 1, and that Westsource checked the box indicating Project 1 was a continuation from a prior year.

Rejection of "Constructive Possession": Actual or constructive knowledge by the Minister via a related corporation's tax return or prior-year filings does not satisfy subsection 37(11). The statutory obligation rests strictly on the claiming taxpayer to include all prescribed information on its own prescribed form.
Principles of Statutory Interpretation vs. Extrinsic Budget Material & Equitable Relief: Unambiguous statutory text governs over general budget statements and equitable pleas.
Argued that federal budget documents showed subsection 37(11) was only meant to prevent late retroactive claims, and submitted that the result was harsh in its particular circumstances.

Textual Primacy & No Equitable Jurisdiction: Extrinsic budget statements cannot override unambiguous statutory text. Facilitating tax administration by enforcing filing rules is a core legislative objective alongside encouraging R&D, and Courts cannot grant relief based on fairness alone.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the appellate holdings of Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen (2018 FCA 57) into actionable tax and engineering governance protocols, the following two applied industry case studies model realistic Canadian corporate scenarios confronting the exact legal, structural, and evidentiary pitfalls identified by the Federal Court of Appeal. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure project governance, contractual terms, technical Form T661 documentation, and contemporaneous experimentation tracking to satisfy statutory SR&ED requirements.
Case Study 1: Intra-Group Collaborative SR&ED Between a Management Holding Corporation and an Operating Manufacturing Subsidiary
Industry Scenario and the Westsource Pitfall

PrairieTech Group Holdings Ltd. ("PrairieTech Holdings") is a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) headquartered in Regina, Saskatchewan, with a December 31 fiscal year-end. PrairieTech Holdings owns 100% of the issued voting shares of PrairieTech Heavy Equipment Solutions Inc. ("PrairieTech Solutions"), an operating industrial manufacturing company that designs and fabricates specialized hydraulic trenching and sub-surface soil stabilization machinery for pipeline and utility installations across Western Canada. During the 2025 taxation year—the second year of a two-year R&D initiative designated internally as "Project ArcticValve"—the two corporations collaborated to develop a novel electro-hydraulic proportional valve manifold capable of maintaining micro-millimetre actuator precision at extreme ambient temperatures of −45°C without hydraulic fluid cavitating or elastomeric seals vitrifying.

Within this corporate structure, PrairieTech Holdings employs the Chief Technology Officer and two senior control-systems engineers who perform mathematical fluid-dynamics modelling, finite element analysis (FEA), and proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control algorithm design, charging PrairieTech Solutions a monthly flat "Management and Executive Services Fee" under a generic one-page intercompany memorandum. Conversely, PrairieTech Solutions employs the metallurgical technicians, CNC machinists, and field-test engineers who machine the experimental valve manifolds, blend custom low-viscosity synthetic esters, and execute cold-chamber bench trials.

In June 2026, both corporations file their initial 2025 T2 corporate income tax returns on their June 30, 2026 filing-due date without including Form T661, planning to prepare their SR&ED claims later within the 12-month subsection 37(11) reporting window expiring June 30, 2027. In May 2027, PrairieTech Solutions files an amended T2 return with a fully populated Form T661 claiming $185,000 in qualified expenditures and $64,750 in RITCs, including complete narratives in Lines 242, 244, and 246 of Part 2. Concurrently, the external accountant for PrairieTech Holdings prepares an amended 2025 T2 return for the parent company to claim $110,000 in specified employee and engineering salaries ($38,500 in associated RITCs) for its contribution to Project ArcticValve. Because Project ArcticValve was already claimed by PrairieTech Holdings in 2024 and because PrairieTech Solutions has just submitted the comprehensive 2025 technical narrative for Project ArcticValve to the CRA, the accountant checks the "continuation of a previously claimed project" box in Part 2, Section A of PrairieTech Holdings' Form T661, inserts a cross-reference to the subsidiary's Business Number in the project title header, and leaves Lines 242, 244, and 246 blank.

Under Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen (2018 FCA 57), PrairieTech Holdings' entire $110,000 expenditure claim and $38,500 RITC will be automatically disallowed by the CRA after June 30, 2027, under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), 37(12), and paragraph 127(9)(m). Furthermore, even if the form had been populated, the generic "Management Services Fee" contract exposes the corporate group to secondary disallowances regarding whether PrairieTech Holdings was performing SR&ED on its own behalf or merely providing routine administrative management, and whether non-arm's length contract payment reductions apply under subsections 127(18) to (20).
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Pre-Filing Compliance Controls

To eliminate procedural forfeiture risk under Westsource, PrairieTech Group must first terminate the practice of filing initial T2 returns with nil SR&ED schedules followed by eleventh-hour T661 amendments near the 18-month mark. Corporate tax governance must mandate that Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 be compiled, reviewed by tax counsel, and transmitted concurrently with the original T2 return on or before the paragraph 150(1)(a) filing-due date (six months post-fiscal year-end, or June 30, 2026). Filing at Month 6 preserves a full 12-month safety buffer prior to the subsection 37(11) statutory bar, allowing any administrative or formatting deficiency flagged during initial CRA assessment to be cured by way of a valid amended Form T661 before the 18-month deadline expires.

Additionally, prior to electronic transmission, the corporate controller and SR&ED advisor must execute a formal verification of Part 8 (Claim Checklist) of Form T661. Internal compliance policy must strictly prohibit the electronic transmission of any Schedule 60 (T2SCH60) where Line 242, Line 244, or Line 246 is blank or contains cross-references to another taxpayer's Business Number or prior-year T661 in lieu of substantive, entity-specific technical descriptions.
Step 2: Restructuring Contractual Terms and Intercompany SR&ED Arrangements

To ensure that the collaborative relationship between PrairieTech Holdings and PrairieTech Solutions aligns with the Income Tax Act and avoids both the Westsource trap and non-arm's length expenditure disallowances, the generic "Management Services Agreement" must be replaced prior to the start of the fiscal year with one of two legally rigorous contractual structures.

Under the first structural option—a Consolidated Operating-Entity Payroll Structure—PrairieTech Group can transfer the employment contracts of the Chief Technology Officer and the two senior control-systems engineers directly onto the payroll of the operating subsidiary, PrairieTech Solutions, while entering into an administrative shared-services cost-recovery agreement solely for the non-R&D executive management time spent by the CTO on holding company governance. By consolidating all R&D personnel inside PrairieTech Solutions, only one corporation (PrairieTech Solutions) incurs SR&ED expenditures and files Form T661 for Project ArcticValve, consolidating 100% of the eligible salary base and Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Part 5 into a single corporate claimant and eliminating dual-entity T661 filing risk entirely.

Conversely, if corporate or commercial reasons require the systems engineers to remain employed by PrairieTech Holdings while both entities file independent T661 claims, the two corporations must execute a formal written Joint Collaborative Research and Cost-Sharing Agreement. This agreement must explicitly sever routine corporate management services (accounting, human resources, and executive governance billed under a separate administrative service schedule) from SR&ED engineering activities. Crucially, to prevent intercompany payments from being characterized as a reimbursement or contract payment that grinds down PrairieTech Holdings' qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18), the contract must stipulate that each corporation bears its own unreimbursed financial risk for its respective R&D work package in exchange for co-ownership or defined licensing royalties in the resulting intellectual property. Schedule A of the contract must explicitly assign Work Package 1 (Thermo-Fluid Mathematical Modelling & Adaptive PID Control Synthesis) exclusively to PrairieTech Holdings, and Work Package 2 (Metallurgical Manifold Fabrication, Seal Formulation & Cryogenic Chamber Testing) exclusively to PrairieTech Solutions.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Entity-Specific Form T661 (Part 2) Drafting

Where PrairieTech Holdings files its own Form T661 under the Joint Collaborative Research structure, tax counsel and the lead systems engineer must draft a complete, standalone Part 2, Section B narrative on PrairieTech Holdings' Schedule 60 (Form T661). To satisfy Lines 242, 244, and 246 independently of its subsidiary's filing and distinctly from its 2024 prior-year claim, the narrative must be structured around the exact mathematical and control-systems work performed by PrairieTech Holdings during 2025.

In Line 242 (Scientific or Technological Uncertainties – Maximum 350 Words), PrairieTech Holdings must articulate the specific mathematical, algorithmic, and control-theory uncertainties faced by its systems engineers in the 2025 taxation year, explaining why 2024 baseline models failed. The compliant narrative on PrairieTech Holdings' Form T661 states:

"While 2024 steady-state modelling established basic fluid viscosity curves at −30°C, a fundamental system-level technological uncertainty emerged in 2025 when attempting to achieve sub-millimetre spool positioning (±0.05 mm with < 12 ms latency) across a transient thermal gradient of −45°C to +15°C. Standard linear PID control laws and conventional Navier-Stokes computational fluid dynamics (CFD) packages could not predict or compensate for non-linear bulk modulus degradation and localized micro-cavitation induced by rapid shear heating of synthetic ester fluids passing through sub-millimetre metering orifices at −45°C. Specifically, it was technologically uncertain whether a real-time, state-space observer algorithm could mathematically decouple non-linear elastomeric seal stiction forces from fluid compressibility phase-lags using only upstream pressure and coil-current feedback, without introducing high-frequency control oscillation (chatter) that destabilizes the hydraulic actuator."

In Line 244 (Work Performed in the Tax Year to Overcome the Uncertainties – Maximum 700 Words), PrairieTech Holdings must chronologically detail the systematic investigation—specifically the hypotheses formulated, simulations and analytical experiments executed by PrairieTech Holdings' engineers during 2025, data analyzed, and iterative modifications made. The compliant narrative on PrairieTech Holdings' Form T661 states:

"In the 2025 taxation year, PrairieTech Holdings' control-systems engineering team conducted a systematic investigation across three iterative experimental phases to resolve the non-linear cryogenic control uncertainty. Under Hypothesis 1 (Q1 2025), the team hypothesized that augmenting a gain-scheduled PID controller with a LuGre dynamic friction model parameterized by fluid temperature would eliminate spool hunting at −45°C. The engineers constructed a coupled multi-physics simulation in MATLAB/Simulink integrating non-Newtonian shear-thinning equations across 140 virtual test runs. Analysis of telemetry transferred from bench trials showed the LuGre model diverged by 38% during rapid pressure transients (> 200 bar/s) due to unmodelled localized adiabatic heating within the valve boundary layer, falsifying Hypothesis 1. Under Hypothesis 2 (Q2–Q3 2025), the team hypothesized that a Sliding Mode Control (SMC) architecture incorporating a real-time Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to estimate effective fluid bulk modulus from solenoid back-EMF ripple could compensate for boundary-layer viscosity drops. The engineers derived a 7th-order state-space differential equation model and executed 65 hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) analytical experiments comparing predicted spool displacement against empirical laser-interferometer logs collected from cold-chamber runs at −40°C and −45°C. While steady-state accuracy improved to ±0.06 mm, EKF covariance wind-up during zero-velocity crossings induced 45 Hz limit-cycle oscillations. Under Hypothesis 3 (Q4 2025), the team modified the hypothesis by replacing the standard signum switching function in the SMC with a continuous boundary-layer hyperbolic tangent function coupled with an adaptive forgetting-factor recursive least-squares (RLS) estimator. Across 48 systematic HIL validation trials, this hybrid RLS-SMC algorithm successfully suppressed chattering by 89% and maintained ±0.04 mm spool tracking accuracy down to −45°C."

In Line 246 (Scientific or Technological Advancements Achieved or Attempted – Maximum 350 Words), PrairieTech Holdings must state the new conceptual technological knowledge gained in 2025 regarding the underlying physical and control-theory phenomena. The compliant narrative on PrairieTech Holdings' Form T661 states:

"Through the systematic investigation conducted in 2025, PrairieTech Holdings achieved a significant technological advancement in extreme-cold electro-hydraulic control systems theory. Specifically, the engineering team generated new predictive knowledge demonstrating that in sub-zero synthetic ester regimes (−40°C to −45°C), localized shear-induced adiabatic heating within micro-orifices alters effective fluid bulk modulus up to 4.2 times faster than bulk reservoir thermal sensors can detect. PrairieTech Holdings established a novel mathematical correlation linking solenoid current back-EMF harmonic distortion directly to transient orifice viscosity gradients, enabling real-time, sensorless state estimation via a 7th-order RLS-Sliding Mode Control architecture that overcomes non-linear cryogenic stiction without destabilizing actuator phase margins."
Step 4: Contemporaneous Experimentation and Financial Tracking

To substantiate Part 2, Section C (Lines 270–282 check-boxes regarding contemporaneous evidence) and Part 3/Part 6 expenditure allocations during a CRA technical and financial review, PrairieTech Holdings must maintain its own entity-segregated digital SR&ED dossier. This dossier must archive dated Simulink model versions, MATLAB script commits, mathematical derivation notebooks, and bi-weekly engineering review minutes explicitly authored by PrairieTech Holdings' employees and cross-referenced to the three hypotheses described in Line 244. Concurrently, rather than relying on year-end percentage estimates, PrairieTech Holdings' engineers must log daily hours into a time-tracking system coded directly to Project ArcticValve's specific experimental tasks—strictly distinguishing core experimental analysis under subsection 248(1) from excluded administrative management duties—reconciled directly to PrairieTech Holdings' T4 payroll summaries and Lines 300 and 305 of Form T661.
Case Study 2: Multi-Project Enterprise Software & AI Claimant Navigating Multi-Year Continuation Projects and the CRA "20-Project" Filing Threshold
Industry Scenario and the Westsource Pitfall

OntariCloud Analytics Corp. ("OntariCloud") is a growth-stage software-as-a-service (SaaS) and distributed artificial intelligence corporation based in Waterloo, Ontario, with a September 30 fiscal year-end, making its T2 corporate filing-due date March 31 and its 12-month subsection 37(11) SR&ED reporting deadline March 31 of the following calendar year. During its taxation year ended September 30, 2025, OntariCloud's 65 software engineers worked in agile two-week sprints across 26 internal micro-projects aimed at building a low-latency, privacy-preserving federated graph neural network (GNN) engine. In early March 2027—just three weeks before the March 31, 2027 statutory reporting bar for its 2025 taxation year—OntariCloud engages an external boutique contingency-fee SR&ED consultant to rush-file an amended 2025 T2 return claiming $2,400,000 in qualified SR&ED expenditures across all 26 micro-projects.

Pressed for time before the March 31, 2027 deadline, the external consultant and OntariCloud's VP of Engineering commit three critical errors that directly trigger the Westsource disallowance doctrine. First, for the 4 largest projects by dollar value ($950,000 of the $2.4M expenditure pool)—which are multi-year core architecture initiatives that were audited in detail by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) for the 2024 taxation year and accepted in full in a written CRA SR&ED Review Report issued in late 2025—the consultant assumes the CRA RTA already possesses the complete architectural blueprints and multi-year roadmap. Consequently, the consultant enters the project titles, project codes, and Part 6 costs on the 2025 Form T661, checks "Continuation" in Line 208 of Part 2, and inserts a one-sentence placeholder in Lines 242, 244, and 246 stating that all technical uncertainties, systematic work, and advancements remain as documented in the CRA 2024 RTA Technical Review Report on file with the Minister.

Second, for the remaining 22 micro-projects ($1,450,000 in expenditures), the tax preparation software only permits electronic transmission of 20 Schedule 60 (Part 2) records (4 of which were occupied by the placeholder continuation projects, leaving 16 slots). The consultant writes hasty Part 2 narratives for 16 micro-projects, lists all 26 projects and their costs in Part 6 (Project Costs), and submits the return on March 30, 2027—without ever drafting or storing completed Part 2 forms at OntariCloud's place of business for the remaining 6 micro-projects ($380,000 in expenditures). Third, in the rush to transmit on March 30, 2027, the consultant leaves Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) incomplete regarding the contingency fee billing arrangement.

Under Westsource (2018 FCA 57), the consequences for OntariCloud are severe. For the 4 core continuation projects ($950,000 in expenditures), the one-sentence cross-reference to the prior year's CRA RTA audit file provides zero prescribed information regarding the work performed in the 2025 taxation year. The Minister's possession of the 2024 RTA report is legally irrelevant; once March 31, 2027 passes, the $950,000 expenditure claim is permanently extinguished under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m). Similarly, for the 6 micro-projects omitted under the "Top 20" rule ($380,000 in expenditures), when the CRA requests their completed Part 2 forms upon initial screening pursuant to Section 4.1 of the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, OntariCloud cannot produce completed Part 2 forms, resulting in immediate disallowance of all $380,000. Finally, for the Part 9 omission, while the remaining 16 projects are not disallowed solely due to Part 9, OntariCloud and the consultant are jointly and severally liable for a $1,000 penalty under subsection 162(5.1).
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and System-Level Project Aggregation

A foundational technical error made by software claimants is equating every Jira epic or agile feature branch with a separate "SR&ED project" on Form T661. As the CRA's Guide to Form T661 (T4088) and Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives stipulate, an "SR&ED project" comprises a set of interrelated activities that collectively are necessary to resolve the scientific or technological uncertainties in the attempt to achieve the specific scientific or technological advancements defined for the project, and the CRA determines eligibility at the system level necessary to recognize all required work, including support work.

By conducting a technical taxonomy review at fiscal year-end (September 30, 2025), OntariCloud's Chief Architect and tax advisor can consolidate the 26 fragmented micro-projects—which were actually interdependent sub-modules and experimental iterations of four overarching architectural challenges—into 4 comprehensive, system-level SR&ED projects. Consolidating 26 micro-claims into 4 system-level projects brings the entire claim well below the 20-project electronic filing threshold of T2SCH60, ensuring that 100% of claimed expenditures in Part 6 are backed by a fully populated Part 2 narrative transmitted directly within the T2 return and eliminating any reliance on the CRA's "Top 20 Projects" administrative exception.
Step 2: Restructuring Third-Party Claim Preparer Contract Terms

To protect the corporation from consultant delays and statutory deadlines, OntariCloud must overhaul its external SR&ED engagement contract to mandate delivery of complete, final-draft Form T661 narratives (Lines 242, 244, and 246 for every claimed project) no later than 45 days prior to the paragraph 150(1)(a) corporate filing-due date (i.e., by February 14, 2026, for the September 30, 2025 year-end), or at an absolute minimum, 90 days prior to the subsection 37(11) 18-month statutory bar.

Furthermore, the engagement contract must contain an explicit warranty and covenant by the claim preparer that no project listed in Part 6 of Form T661 will be filed without a complete, fiscal-year-specific technical narrative in Lines 242, 244, and 246 of Part 2; that no cross-references to prior-year filings, CRA RTA reports, or affiliated entity returns will be substituted for substantive technical text; and that any contingency fee otherwise payable is forfeited—and professional errors-and-omissions indemnification is triggered—if any project is disallowed under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), or 37(12) for incomplete prescribed information. The contract must also pre-populate the exact Part 9 prescribed fields required under paragraph 37(11)(b) and subsection 162(5.3)—specifically the claim preparer's Business Number, billing arrangement code, and certification signature—ensuring zero exposure to the subsection 162(5.1) $1,000 penalty.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Year-Over-Year Narrative Differentiation for Continuation Projects

For multi-year software projects where Line 208 indicates a continuation from a prior taxation year, Westsource confirms that prior-year CRA knowledge does not excuse current-year disclosure on Form T661. Moreover, simply copying and pasting the prior year's Line 242, 244, and 246 text into the current year's Form T661 invites a CRA audit challenge that no new systematic progression occurred during the current year. OntariCloud must implement a Delta-Progression Narrative Protocol for Lines 242, 244, and 246 on Form T661.

In Line 242 (Scientific or Technological Uncertainties – Maximum 350 Words), OntariCloud must frame the opening sentences around the baseline state of knowledge achieved at the close of Fiscal 2024 (September 30, 2024), and dedicate the remainder of the field to the new or unresolved technological uncertainties encountered during Fiscal 2025 (October 1, 2024 – September 30, 2025). The compliant narrative on OntariCloud's Form T661 states:

"At the conclusion of FY2024, OntariCloud's experimental prototype established basic homomorphic encryption wrappers for static 2-hop graph neural network (GNN) message passing across 10 nodes. However, when scaling to dynamic, streaming heterogeneous graphs exceeding 10<sup>7</sup> edges across 50 asynchronous edge-compute nodes in FY2025, a fundamental computer science uncertainty emerged regarding Byzantine-resilient gradient aggregation under strict tail-latency constraints (p99 < 40 ms). Existing federated learning protocols (such as FedAvg and Krum) and standard differential privacy noise-injection mechanisms caused catastrophic gradient explosion and representation collapse (over-smoothing) beyond 4 GNN layers when non-IID (non-independent and identically distributed) subgraph topologies mutated dynamically. It was technologically uncertain whether a novel spectral graph sparsification algorithm could be mathematically unified with zero-knowledge ring-LWE (Learning With Errors) ciphertext packing to bound Byzantine poisoning error without exceeding memory bandwidth limits (16 GB VRAM) on edge nodes."

In Line 244 (Work Performed in the Tax Year to Overcome the Uncertainties – Maximum 700 Words), OntariCloud must detail exclusively the hypotheses formulated, experimental code architectures built, benchmark datasets tested, and empirical failure metrics recorded between October 1, 2024, and September 30, 2025. The compliant narrative on OntariCloud's Form T661 states:

"Between October 2024 and September 2025, OntariCloud's distributed systems team executed a systematic investigation comprising four major experimental iterations. In Iteration 1 (Oct–Dec 2024 – Spectral Chebyshev Polynomial Approximation), the team hypothesized that approximating graph Laplacian convolutions via 3rd-order Chebyshev polynomials prior to ring-LWE encryption would bound ciphertext expansion while preserving topological variance. Engineers implemented experimental C++/CUDA kernels (commit-tag: sred-fy25-exp1) and benchmarked across 12 synthetic non-IID temporal graphs (5 × 10<sup>6</sup> edges). Empirical results showed p99 latency reached 185 ms due to polynomial multiplication depth exhausting the ciphertext noise budget, triggering mandatory bootstrapping every 2 epochs and refuting the first hypothesis. In Iteration 2 (Jan–Mar 2025 – Stochastic Resistance-Distance Sparsification), the team formulated a second hypothesis that dynamically pruning inter-node boundary edges using effective resistance-distance sampling before gradient encryption would eliminate bootstrapping overhead without degrading F1 classification accuracy. Across 34 controlled cluster experiments varying sampling thresholds (ε ∈ [0.05, 0.40]), data analysis revealed that while latency dropped to 52 ms, asynchronous node stragglers introduced stale-gradient bias that degraded minority-class recall by 24.6% under simulated 15% Byzantine node corruption. In Iteration 3 (Apr–Jul 2025 – Delay-Compensated Geometric Median Aggregation in Ciphertext Domain), the team hypothesized that formulating an approximate Weiszfeld geometric median estimator operating directly on quantized CRT (Chinese Remainder Theorem) residue channels could reject Byzantine outliers while compensating for asynchronous staleness via Taylor-series Hessian approximations. Executing 50 systematic A/B benchmark runs across a 48-node Kubernetes testbed revealed numerical underflow in the 32-bit CRT residue moduli when staleness exceeded 5 iterations. In Iteration 4 (Aug–Sep 2025 – Mixed-Precision Residue Number System [RNS] Scaling), the team modified the mathematical formulation by implementing dynamic RNS base-extension scaling coupled with variance-reduced stochastic gradient tracking. Across 28 validation runs, this architecture resolved the numerical underflow, achieved p99 aggregation latency of 34.2 ms, and maintained 94.1% F1 convergence under 20% Byzantine adversarial perturbation."

In Line 246 (Scientific or Technological Advancements Achieved or Attempted – Maximum 350 Words), OntariCloud must articulate the specific advancement in computer science and distributed systems engineering achieved during Fiscal 2025. The compliant narrative on OntariCloud's Form T661 states:

"In FY2025, OntariCloud achieved a major technological advancement in distributed cryptographic machine learning by demonstrating how to perform Byzantine-resilient geometric median gradient aggregation on dynamic, non-IID graph neural networks within a non-interactive ring-LWE ciphertext space. Specifically, the engineering team discovered the mathematical boundary conditions under which 32-bit CRT residue channels suffer precision collapse during asynchronous Taylor-series staleness compensation, and developed a novel mixed-precision RNS base-extension algorithm integrated with resistance-distance spectral sparsification that reduces cryptographic communication overhead by 78% while bounding adversarial drift."
Step 4: Contemporaneous Experimentation Tracking in Agile Environments

To ensure that OntariCloud can both generate its Part 2 narratives before its 6-month T2 filing-due date and defend the claim during a CRA technical review, the engineering organization must embed automated SR&ED hypothesis tracking directly into its DevOps workflow. By configuring Jira and GitHub Issues so that any engineering ticket linked to an SR&ED epic requires four mandatory custom metadata fields before a pull request can be merged—specifically Technological Uncertainty Targeted, Hypothesis Statement, Benchmark Test Protocol & Metrics, and Logical Conclusion / Failure Analysis—contemporaneous documentation is generated organically as the code progresses. At the close of each fiscal quarter (Q1 through Q4), the automated logs from these SR&ED epics are exported into a living draft of Form T661 Part 2 (Lines 242, 244, and 246), ensuring that by the time the fiscal year closes on September 30, the prescribed technical narrative is already written, verified by the lead engineers who performed the work, and ready for inclusion on Form T661 well ahead of the statutory deadline.

cells: Primary Westsource Vulnerability
Leaving Lines 242, 244, and 246 blank on the parent holding company's Form T661 while relying on the operating subsidiary's accepted Form T661 for the same collaborative project.
Substituting one-sentence references to a prior-year CRA RTA audit report on 4 continuation projects, and failing to prepare Part 2 forms for 6 micro-projects beyond the 20-project e-filing limit.
Governance & Filing Restructuring
Mandatory concurrent filing of Form T661 with the initial T2 return at Month 6 (June 30), preserving a 12-month curative amendment buffer prior to the Month 18 subsection 37(11) statutory bar.
Aggregating 26 fragmented agile micro-projects into 4 system-level SR&ED projects under subsection 248(1), bringing the entire claim within the 20-project electronic transmission threshold.
Contractual & Structural Remedy
Replacing the generic flat-fee Management Services Agreement with either consolidated subsidiary payroll or a formal Joint Collaborative Research Agreement partitioning distinct Work Packages.
Inserting contractual delivery milestones (45 days prior to T2 filing-due date), fee forfeiture/indemnity clauses for subsection 37(11) omissions, and mandatory Part 9 preparer disclosures.
Technical Form T661 Narrative Protocol
Drafting standalone, entity-specific Lines 242, 244, and 246 narratives restricted strictly to the parent company's thermo-fluid mathematical modelling and Sliding Mode Control algorithm synthesis.
Implementing a Delta-Progression Narrative Protocol that explicitly separates prior-year baseline architecture from current-year hypotheses, failed iterations, and empirical metrics.
Contemporaneous Evidence & Tracking
Entity-segregated digital binders archiving MATLAB/Simulink commits and daily engineering time-sheets coded to specific experimental tasks versus excluded management duties.
Mandatory Jira/GitHub pull-request metadata fields capturing hypotheses and benchmark test results in real time, synthesized quarterly into draft Part 2 narratives.

body.text: 5. Synthesis and Strategic Advisory Conclusions

The Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. Her Majesty The Queen, 2018 FCA 57, delivers an unmistakable doctrinal directive to Canadian corporate taxpayers, chief financial officers, R&D directors, and tax practitioners: in the administration of Canada's SR&ED tax incentive regime, procedural form and substantive technical disclosure are legally indivisible. Subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12), together with paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, do not merely establish a deadline for reporting financial expenditure pools; they establish an inflexible statutory condition precedent requiring the taxpayer to plead its prima facie technical case—specifically technological uncertainty (Line 242), systematic investigation in the taxation year (Line 244), and technological advancement (Line 246)—directly on the face of its own Form T661 within 12 months of its corporate filing-due date.

Consequently, a corporate claimant can never rely on the Minister's actual or constructive possession of technical information located outside the four corners of that specific taxpayer's Form T661 for that specific taxation year. Neither the acceptance of an identical collaborative project narrative in a related corporation's tax return nor the existence of prior-year CRA audit reports for a continuing multi-year project cures a blank or placeholder Part 2 narrative. Because subsection 37(12) deems any expenditure lacking timely prescribed information not to be an SR&ED expenditure for all purposes of the Act, and because neither the Minister nor the Courts can grant relief based on equitable fairness or extrinsic budgetary intent, filing Form T661 near the end of the 18-month post-year-end window carries asymmetrical catastrophic risk. Best-in-class corporate tax governance demands consolidating interrelated technical activities into well-defined system-level projects, structuring intercompany R&D agreements to avoid multi-entity duplication, and filing a fully populated Form T661 concurrently with the original T2 corporate income tax return at the 6-month filing-due date to preserve a full 12-month curative window prior to the statutory bar.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; FCA found no reviewable error in the Tax Court's conclusion that the projects were routine engineering.
